title: Asymmetric batch windowing and MoE gating interference - investigation notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures experiments and profiling traces exploring a recurring tail-latency pattern we see with long-context MoE workloads: when requests in a batch have highly asymmetric sequence lengths (a few long sequences >> most short sequences) the MoE gating and KV-cache subsystems interact in ways that sharply increase per-token 95th/99th latency. The behavior is model-architecture- and implementation-sensitive: Llama-family dense runs show different hotspots from Mistral/Qwen and MoE variants amplify a few issues (gating scatter/gather, expert memory thrash).

Why this matters:
- Real customer workloads (chat+tooling with occasional document dumps) produce asymmetric batches frequently.
- Degraded tail latency at high-percentiles directly violates SLOs and causes degraded UX even if p50 looks fine.
- Identifying mitigations with minimal cost increases is critical for Dedicated and Private customers.

Models / Hardware used:
- Llama-2-13B (dense) on 1x A100-80GB (single-GPU runs)
- Mistral-7B (dense) on A100 and H100 testbeds
- Qwen-7B (dense) on H100 (to compare attention kernel behavior)
- MoE-70B-equivalent topology (12k experts sharded across 4xA100s in our cluster sim) for gating-specific runs
- Serving runtime build: runtime@main + PR #1792 (gating prefetch), kernels: cuBLAS/cuDNN default, custom fused-gather v2 enabled

Workload patterns tested:
- Baseline uniform: batch of 8 requests, all length 512 tokens (warm cache)
- Asymmetric-1: batch 8, 1 request length 8192, others length 64
- Asymmetric-2: batch 16, 2 requests length 4096, others length 8
- Streaming vs non-streaming tokens: check impact of incremental KV writes

Key observed phenomena (through profiler traces + wall times):
1) Gating-induced write amplification (MoE-specific)
- When a long request arrives, gating fanout for that request can trigger large expert activation writes. Because routing/sharding is per-request and our IO path batches writes at per-batch granularity, the presence of a long request causes repeated large scatter ops that interleave with short-request work.
- Trace shows many small host->device memcpy launches when the long-request's experts are hot; these memcpys coincide with CUDA stream syncs, causing short requests to stall behind long-request scatter steps.
- Wall time: asymmetric-1 p95 increases ~3.6x compared to baseline on the same config.

2) KV-cache shadowing and read amplification (dense + MoE)
- Long sequences cause our KV cache prefetch window to be extended; when combined with more aggressive prefix-check caching, we observe higher cache invalidation churn. Short requests in the same batch see increased KV lookup latencies because the GPU memory bus becomes saturated by long-request KV reads/writes.
- Profiling shows 40–60% of the additional GPU time is spent in KV gather and non-fused attention index ops.

3) Kernel-launch vs compute imbalance for attention kernels (model-specific)
- Llama kernels show higher effective occupancy and are compute-heavy; the asymmetry problem is largely IO (KV) and memory coalescing.
- Mistral attention kernels are more launch-heavy at small sequence lengths due to many small tiled kernels; adding long sequences increases scheduler churn and increases host-side latency.
- Qwen shows efficient long-window attention but is sensitive to attention index compression path; when attention index compression kicks in for long sequences it reallocates buffers in-place leading to transient fragmentation and CUDA OOM-like stalls (not real OOM).

4) PCIe/NIC saturation on multi-GPU MoE sharded expert fanout
- In our 4xA100 sharded MoE runs, asymmetric batches cause bursty PCIe traffic as the long request fans out to many experts across GPUs. Short requests that require cross-GPU expert results suffer added latency because the interconnect queues spike intermittently.
- Instruments show 30–45% link utilization spikes during long-request fanout windows.

Repro steps (short):
- Checkout runtime@main + PR #1792, build with fused-gather=on, gating-prefetch=on
- Run perf harness: ./tools/bench_batch --model moe_4xA100 --batch 8 --seqs "8192,64,64,64,64,64,64,64" --warm 4 --iters 30
- Capture trace with nvtx + runtime profiler: ./tools/run_trace.sh --out /tmp/trace.json
- Observe stream syncs around gating::scatter and kvcache::gather ops

Profiling snippets (condensed):
- nvprof timeline: repeated small memcpy launches (avg 12–18 us) at gating scatter points; GPU compute kernels sit idle waiting for memcpys
- runtime counters: kvcache_misses++ correlated to long-request prefix positions; cache invalidations temporally overlap with gating scatter

Hypotheses for root cause (ranked):
1) Our gating implementation emits many small scatter/gather operations instead of coalesced batched ops when batch contains mixed-length sequences. This leads to many host->device operations and stream syncs.
2) KV cache prefetch policy extends prefetch horizons for long sequences without accounting for mixed-batch effects; prefetches displace working set for short requests.
3) Expert placement is not topology-aware at shard assignment time for dynamic long-request fanouts, causing unnecessary cross-GPU transfers.

Short-term mitigations tested (and results):
- Gating coalesce buffer: buffer per-GPU gating indices for the whole batch and emit one fused scatter/gather: reduces p95 by ~30% in asymmetric-1, but increases steady-state memory footprint by ~6%.
- Gating cooldown (rate-limit fanout from very-long requests): reduces PCIe spikes but increases long-request latency; p95 for short requests improved by 40%, overall batch p95 tradeoff requires policy tuning.
- Prefix-aware KV reservation: allocate an isolated KV slab for long-request prefetches to avoid evicting short-request working set; reduces KV read stalls for short requests, p95 short-request latency down ~25%.

Medium-term engineering proposals:
- Implement fused gather-scatter kernels at the runtime layer to avoid tens-to-hundreds of small memcpys. Prioritize a GPU-resident batched routing table and single large gather per expert per-batch.
- Topology-aware expert co-location policy: when a request's gate predicts >N experts on remote GPUs, prefer local expert fallback or re-route via cached expert replicas to minimize cross-GPU traffic.
- Mixed-batch scheduler heuristics: detect asymmetric-batch patterns and split into micro-batches (process long requests in small dedicated micro-batches or run long sequences in a separate pipeline with relaxed latency SLOs). Add an admission controller that can opt to process long requests outside latency-critical lanes.
- Adaptive KV prefetch window: shorten prefetch horizon when mixed-batch detected or when cache pressure metric exceeds threshold. Consider multi-slab KV layout (short-request slab vs long-request slab) with different eviction policies.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How much of the gating memcopy overhead is due to host-side index sorting versus device-side scattering? (Need a microbenchmark that isolates host sort cost.)
- Can we design a light-weight admission control that is acceptable to product (user-visible delay vs improved p99 for interactive users)?
- Quantization interaction: does int8 quantization reduce memory bandwidth enough to materially help these contention cases? We should benchmark single-GPU quantized MoE inference and observe whether kernel fragmentation changes.
- PR #1792 gating prefetch helped in some cases but made asymmetric p95 worse in others; need to add integration tests that include mixed-length synthetic batches.

Quick experiment plan (next 2 weeks):
1) Microbenchmark fused-gather vs current per-example scatter (team: Luca + Jin). Target: get a 2x reduction in number of memcpys per batch on A100.
2) Implement and run topology-aware expert placement simulation (team: Ethan) across our 4xA100 cluster image to quantify PCIe reductions.
3) Add a mixed-batch test suite in CI (team: Samira) that runs asymmetric workloads nightly and flags regressions.
4) Product sync to scope an admission control policy (PM + SE) — deliver a short spec for opt-in degraded-latency lane for document ingestion.

Notes / anecdotal logs:
- Slack thread G87392J has a user report with a customer trace that matches our synthetic asymmetric-1 pattern. Customer uses chat + occasional transcript ingestion.
- Observed on H100 the same pattern but with lower absolute numbers; however, stream synchronization latencies are more brittle on H100 scheduling leading to occasional host OOM when we naively increase coalesce buffers.

Appendix: quick commands and traces to reproduce locally:
- ./tools/bench_batch --model moe_4xA100 --batch 8 --seqs '8192,64,64,64,64,64,64,64' --output perf.log
- ./tools/run_trace.sh --trace perf.log --nvtx --out /tmp/asym_trace.json
- grep -E 'scatter|kvcache' /tmp/asym_trace.json | sed -n '1,120p'

If you are assigned: please add short experimental notes (what changed, dates, diff link) to this doc. I will iterate on a final set of mitigations once we have microbench numbers.

-- Samira
